title: Fear among Syrians: A Proposed Cutoff Score for the Arabic Fear of COVID-19 Scale

genuine.note: A study of PTSD, emotion dysregulation and alcohol use among US college students is cited for Syria entering its third COVID-19 wave; it has nothing on Syria or COVID-19. Probably the wrong reference (only the abstract was available, off-topic tag from both pipelines).

false_alarm.note: The Greek validation study states that no optimal cut-off had been proposed before it and proposes one, so at the time it was the only such study, as the sentence says.

Caused by the checker: the resolver matched Kline's SEM textbook to a journal book review with the same title (DOI 10.15353/cgjsc.v1i1.3787) and checked the review; the thresholds are standard and are in the book.
Group citation for a range of Cronbach's alpha values (0.82-0.88) across four studies; the original FCV-19S paper reports 0.82, the lower end.
The Italian validation reports alpha = 0.871, within the cited range across studies.
The Turkish adaptation reports alpha = .847 (and the original .82), within the range; this reference duplicates [42] in the citing paper's own bibliography.
The source documents fleeing health workers, few ventilators and bombed hospitals; 'Syrians must feel constant fear for their lives' is the citing authors' inference, clearly marked as such ('must').

debatable.note: The original Fear of COVID-19 Scale paper (Iranian sample) is a fair example of researchers assessing fear of COVID-19, but on its own it does not show assessments 'in different regions of the world' or identification of triggers.

The source says enumerating all deaths, compared with historically expected mortality, gives a picture of excess death with direct and indirect burdens; the citing sentence swaps in 'the 0.28% crude mortality rate', which is not in the source (possibly from the co-cited [4]).

The source reports severe shortages (about 1 mental health professional per 100,000) and expects most people with mental illness to go untreated; the exact figures (90% unattended, 80 psychiatrists) may come from the co-cited [66].
A garbled sentence defining fear of COVID-19 as a prolonged worry or negative emotional reaction; Van Bavel et al. discuss fear and threat perception in pandemics but give no such definition.

summary_line: Caught 5 of 5 planted errors · 6 false alarms · 1 real citation problem found in the original paper
